Analysis Methods for AI Evaluation

Session 6

2026-10-06

The design sets the analysis

  • Random assignment makes the difference in means an unbiased estimate.
    • Pretreatment information (blocks, pairs, covariates) can make it more precise.
  • How different would it be if we ran the study again?
    • new questions
    • new users
    • new runs on the same questions
    • a new random assignment.
  • Your design fixes which of these happen.
    • Uncertainty measures follow from it.

Your PAP must give the complete analysis recipe: point estimate, standard error, and confidence interval, each justified by the design.

  • “Analyze as you randomize”: attributed to R. A. Fisher (1935, The Design of Experiments).

Where uncertainty comes from

Every estimate comes with a margin of error

  • Your study produces a number: how much changing one piece of the Bundle helps.
  • Different questions, or a different coin flip for who gets which Bundle, would give a different number.
  • This section asks
    • where does that variation come from?
    • how to measure it?
    • how can we conceive of and measure “correctness”?

The running example: retrieval in a course tutor

  • System: an LLM tutor answers course questions. Bundle B adds retrieval over course materials; Bundle A does not.
  • Sample: \(N=100\) questions drawn from the questions students could ask.
  • Assignment: retrieval on for \(m=50\) questions at random. \(Z_i=1\) if question \(i\) gets it.
  • Outcome: a 0–100 score for each answer. Each question is run \(R\) times; \(R=1\) until stated otherwise.

\[Y_{ir}=50+\tau Z_i+a_i+e_{ir},\qquad \operatorname{sd}(a_i)=\sigma_a=8,\quad \operatorname{sd}(e_{ir})=\sigma_e=6,\quad \tau=3.\]

  • \(a_i\): difficulty of question \(i\), shared by all its runs. \(e_{ir}\): run-to-run noise.
  • Indices: \(i=1,\dots,N\) questions; \(r=1,\dots,R\) runs; \(NR\) scored calls.

The difference in means and its design-based variance

  • Estimate: mean score with retrieval minus mean score without.

\[\hat\tau=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0,\qquad \widehat{V}(\hat\tau)=\frac{s_1^2}{m}+\frac{s_0^2}{N-m}.\]

fit <- tidy(difference_in_means(Y ~ Z, data = study))
Estimate SE Lower 95% Upper 95%
2.84 2.05 -1.23 6.9
  • The exact variance also depends on how effects vary across questions.
    • That term is unobservable, so this estimate errs on the large side.
  • \(s_1^2, s_0^2\): sample variances of scores in each group.
  • Gerber & Green (2012), eq. 3.6 (true SE) and 3.7 (conservative estimator).
  • Also called the Neyman variance estimator (Neyman 1923).
  • estimatr::difference_in_means; equals lm_robust with HC2 SEs here.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, eqs. 3.6–3.7.

Two sources of uncertainty: sampling and assignment

Sampling

  • Which questions enter the study.
  • Repeat: draw new questions.
  • Estimand: average effect over the population of questions.

Assignment

  • Which questions get retrieval.
  • Repeat: re-randomize the same questions.
  • Estimand: average effect on these questions.
  • The variance formula above covers both when questions are a random sample.
  • A claim about new questions needs the sampling term.
    • The question set has to be a credible sample of that population.
  • Abadie et al.: clustering is a statement about how sampling or assignment worked.
  • Abadie, Athey, Imbens & Wooldridge (2023), QJE 138(1).
  • SATE: sample average treatment effect. PATE: population average treatment effect.

Abadie, Athey, Imbens & Wooldridge (2023), When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?, QJE 138(1).

Randomization inference

  • Sharp null: each question scores the same with or without retrieval.
  • Re-randomize the 100 questions 2,000 times; recompute the difference each time.
null_diffs <- permutation_draws(study, draws = 2000)
observed <- with(study, mean(Y[Z == 1]) - mean(Y[Z == 0]))
p_value <- mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed))

The red line is the observed difference. Two-sided \(p=0.170\).

  • Gerber & Green (2012), ch. 3.4: randomization inference.
  • ri2 package: conduct_ri() for the same calculation.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, §3.4.

Coverage is the test of a standard error

  • Coverage: the fraction of 95% intervals containing the true effect.
  • Template: repeat the whole design, compute each interval, count the hits.
  • First 100 of 250 studies. Red intervals miss the true 3-point effect.
  • Coverage: 93.6%.
  • Every simulation today reports coverage for a design and a standard error.

Estimate, variance, and coverage

  • Random assignment makes the difference in means unbiased. The Neyman variance gives its standard error from the design alone.
  • Uncertainty has two sources: sampling the questions and assigning treatment. Which ones you count decides whether you learn about the population or about these questions.
  • Randomization inference tests the sharp null using the assignment step alone.
  • Coverage checks any standard error: simulate the design and see whether 95% intervals contain the truth 95% of the time.

Matching standard errors to the design

How to deal with repeated measures

  • Eval data often reuses things:
    • the same question run many times
    • the same graders scoring every answer
  • Measurements that share a question or a grader overlap in what they tell you.
  • Counting each one as fresh evidence makes results look more certain than they are.
  • This section provides tools to accurately reflect uncertainty

A clustered SE sums residuals within each question

  • Mean score over all \(NR\) calls; residual \(\hat e_{ir}=Y_{ir}-\bar Y\).

\[\widehat V_{\text{iid}}(\bar Y)=\frac{1}{(NR)^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat e_{ir}^2,\qquad \widehat V_{\text{cluster}}(\bar Y)=\frac{1}{(NR)^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat e_{ir}\Big)^2.\]

  • Expanding the square adds \(\hat e_{ir}\hat e_{is}\) for every pair of runs \(r\neq s\) on the same question.
    • In the model both residuals contain \(a_i\), so these products average about \(\sigma_a^2>0\).
    • Products across questions are set to zero: questions are the independent units.
  • The approximation needs many clusters: \(N\) questions, not \(NR\) calls, is the sample size.

Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals, eq. 4.

In regression, clustering changes the sandwich

  • Regression: \(\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\beta+\mathbf e\) by OLS. Clusters \(g=1,\dots,G\) (here, questions); \(\mathbf X_g\), \(\hat{\mathbf e}_g\) are cluster \(g\)’s rows and residuals.

\[\widehat V(\hat\beta)=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{g=1}^{G}\mathbf X_g'\hat{\mathbf e}_g\hat{\mathbf e}_g'\mathbf X_g\Big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}.\]

  • The outer terms are the OLS “bread”. The middle “meat” treats each cluster’s score \(\mathbf X_g'\hat{\mathbf e}_g\) as one independent draw.
  • One call per cluster: the meat is \(\sum_i \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i'\hat e_i^2\), the robust (HC0) variance.
  • With \(\mathbf x_i=(1,Z_i)\), the entry for \(\hat\tau\) is the clustered variance of the difference in means.
  • CR2 (the lm_robust default): replace \(\hat{\mathbf e}_g\) with \((\mathbf I_g-\mathbf H_{gg})^{-1/2}\hat{\mathbf e}_g\). \(\mathbf H_{gg}\): cluster \(g\)’s block of \(\mathbf X(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\); \(\mathbf I_g\): identity matrix.

Bell & McCaffrey (2002), Bias Reduction in Standard Errors for Linear Regression with Multi-Stage Samples, Survey Methodology 28(2).

Repeated calls are clustered within questions

  • Running example with \(R=5\): 500 scored calls on 100 questions.
  • Every run of question \(i\) shares \(a_i\). Average the runs of each question:

\[\bar Y_i=50+\tau Z_i+a_i+\bar e_i,\qquad V(\hat\tau)=\Big(\sigma_a^2+\frac{\sigma_e^2}{R}\Big)\Big(\frac1m+\frac1{N-m}\Big).\]

  • More runs shrink only the run-noise term.
  • A call-level SE treats the \(NR\) calls as independent.
    • It uses \((\sigma_a^2+\sigma_e^2)/R\) in place of \(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_e^2/R\).
  • The ratio is the design effect: \(1+(R-1)\rho\), with \(\rho=\sigma_a^2/(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_e^2)\).
    • Here \(\rho=0.64\), \(R=5\): variance ratio 3.6, SE ratio 1.9.

Kish (1965), Survey Sampling, Wiley.

Simulation: call-level standard errors undercover

  • 100 questions; \(R=1,2,5,10\) runs each; 250 studies per point.
  • One run per question: the two SEs coincide.
  • More runs narrow the call-level interval. The clustered interval barely moves, because question difficulty dominates.

Cluster where the design groups units

  • Abadie et al.: the sampling process and the assignment mechanism decide whether and where to cluster.
  • Clustered assignment (all runs of a question, a user, a classroom): cluster at the assignment level.
  • Clustered sampling (passages, questions with repeated runs): cluster at the sampling level.
  • Neither: questions sampled and assigned one at a time. Use robust SEs.
    • Clustering on topic widens intervals for no reason, even if scores within a topic correlate.
  • Treatment varies within sampled clusters, as in pairs: cluster SEs are conservative.
    • The paired SE, or Abadie et al.’s CCV estimator, is tighter.
  • Miller: clustering reading comprehension tasks by passage makes the SE 3× larger.

Abadie, Athey, Imbens & Wooldridge (2023), When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?, QJE 138(1). Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals, Table 4.

Pairs and blocks: compare within, then average

  • Blocks \(j=1,\dots,J\), formed before assignment: \(Y_i=50+\tau Z_i+\gamma_{j(i)}+\epsilon_i\).
    • Randomize within each block; block \(j\) has \(N_j\) questions, \(m_j\) treated.

\[\hat\tau=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{N_j}{N}\hat\tau_j,\qquad \widehat V(\hat\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\Big(\frac{N_j}{N}\Big)^2\Big(\frac{s_{1j}^2}{m_j}+\frac{s_{0j}^2}{N_j-m_j}\Big).\]

  • \(\hat\tau_j\), the difference in means within block \(j\), cancels the shared \(\gamma_j\).
  • Pairs are blocks of two: question \(j\) runs once per Bundle, so \(\hat\tau_j=D_j=Y_{jB}-Y_{jA}\).
    • One unit per arm leaves \(s_{1j}^2\) undefined; use the spread of the \(D_j\):

\[\widehat V(\hat\tau)=\frac{s_D^2}{J},\qquad s_D^2=s_A^2+s_B^2-2s_{AB}.\]

  • Ignoring the pairs drops \(s_{AB}\).

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, §§3.6.1, 4.4. Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals, §4.2.

Simulation: ignoring pairs or blocks

  • Pairs: both Bundles once on 100 questions. Blocks: lecture 05 design, 80 questions in 4 difficulty blocks.
  • Same \(\hat\tau\) either way here. Ignoring the blocks keeps their variation in the SE: intervals stay wide.

Questions and annotators are both sampled

  • Human-scored running example: the same \(K=20\) annotators, drawn from a pool of graders, score all \(N\) answers.

\[Y_{ik}=50+\tau Z_i+a_i+b_k+\gamma_kZ_i+\varepsilon_{ik}.\]

  • \(a_i\): difficulty. \(b_k\): leniency. \(\gamma_k\): how much annotator \(k\) rewards retrieval answers.
  • Target: the effect as judged by new annotators on new questions.

\[V(\hat\tau)\approx\frac{4(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2/K)}{N}+\frac{\sigma_\gamma^2}{K}.\]

  • \(b_k\) cancels: every annotator scores both arms. The \(\gamma_k\) term depends only on the 20 annotators.
  • Westfall et al.: with two crossed samples, power hits a ceiling as one grows. The other’s size sets it.

Westfall, Judd & Kenny (2015), Replicating Studies in Which Samples of Participants Respond to Samples of Stimuli, Perspectives on Psychological Science 10(3).

Simulation: one-way versus two-way clustering

  • 20 annotators; 20 to 500 questions. \(\sigma_a=8\), \(\sigma_b=6\), \(\sigma_\gamma=4\), \(\sigma_\varepsilon=6\).
  • Two-way: \(\widehat V=\widehat V_{\text{question}}+\widehat V_{\text{annotator}}-\widehat V_{\text{score}}\) (sandwiches); \(t_{19}\).
  • Question-only clustering treats the 20 annotators as fixed. Coverage falls as questions are added.

Cameron, Gelbach & Miller (2011), Robust Inference With Multiway Clustering, JBES 29(2).

Small samples break the normal approximation

\[\text{Wald: }\ \hat p\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{N}},\qquad \text{Wilson: }\ \Big\{p:\ |\hat p-p|\le z\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}}\Big\}.\]

  • \(\hat p=x/N\), \(z=1.96\). Wald plugs in \(\hat p\), so 20 of 20 gives \([1,1]\). Wilson uses each candidate \(p\).
  • 95% accuracy, 20 questions: Wald covers 64%, Wilson 92%.

Bowyer, Aitchison & Ivanova (2025), ICML. Wilson (1927), JASA 22(158).

Benchmark scores depend on the questions

  • A benchmark score averages over the questions its authors chose.
    • Its SE assumes they are a random sample from the population you care about.
  • Ailem et al.: model performance is correlated across prompts.
    • Correlations track semantic similarity and shared failure points.
    • Accounting for them changes model rankings on major benchmarks.
  • Perlitz et al.: HELM rankings shift with benchmark design choices.
    • Removing one low-ranked model can change the leader.
  • In your PAP:
    • define the question population and how questions are drawn from it
    • cluster where questions arrive in groups
    • report the effect by topic as a secondary analysis.

Ailem, Marazopoulou, Siska & Bono (2024), Examining the Robustness of LLM Evaluation to the Distributional Assumptions of Benchmarks, ACL. Perlitz et al. (2024), Efficient Benchmarking (of Language Models), NAACL.

Or is a benchmark just a fixed exam?

  • An error bar asks how the score would move with a fresh draw of questions.
  • A benchmark’s questions were chosen, curated, and frozen.
    • There is no population they were drawn from, so the error bar describes an imagined resampling.
  • Recht: benchmarks work as a shared competition. Everyone takes the same exam, and results are reproducible.
  • Recht et al.: a new ImageNet test set, built the same way, cost 11–14 points of accuracy.
    • That drop is far outside any error bar on the original test set.
    • The ranking of models was almost exactly preserved.
  • Uncertainty still matters because deployment is a kind of replication.

Recht (2025), Standard error of what now?, arg min. Recht (2025), Benchmarking our benchmarks, arg min. Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt & Shankar (2019), Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?, ICML.

Standard errors that match the design

  • The standard error must treat as independent exactly the units the design sampled or assigned independently.
  • Repeated runs share a question, so cluster on the question. The design effect says how much call-level SEs understate, and it grows with more runs.
  • Pairs and blocks are compared within, so their SEs drop the shared variation.
  • Sampled questions and sampled annotators are crossed. Two-way clustering counts both, and the smaller sample caps precision.
  • With few units the normal approximation fails. Use small-sample intervals.

Covariates buy precision

Use what you know before the experiment

  • Before the study runs, you often know something about each question: its topic, how hard it was in a pilot.
  • Retrieval cannot change that information, because it was recorded first.
  • Using it in the analysis sharpens the comparison and leaves the target the same.
  • This section shows how to use it.

The Lin estimator: adjust with interactions

  • Freedman (2008): adding covariates to the regression can reduce precision, and its usual SEs can be wrong.
    • The problem arises when treatment changes how covariates relate to the outcome.
  • Lin (2013): center the covariate and interact it with treatment.

\[Y_i=\alpha+\tau Z_i+\beta(X_i-\bar X)+\gamma Z_i(X_i-\bar X)+\varepsilon_i.\]

  • \(\hat\tau\) estimates the average effect.
  • HC2 SE: the sandwich with meat \(\sum_i \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i'\hat\varepsilon_i^2/(1-h_{ii})\); \(\mathbf x_i\) is row \(i\) of the regression, \(h_{ii}\) its leverage.
  • In large samples it is at least as precise as the difference in means.
lm_lin(Y ~ Z, covariates = ~ pretest, data = study)
  • Freedman (2008), Advances in Applied Mathematics 40; Annals of Applied Statistics 2.
  • Lin (2013), Annals of Applied Statistics 7(1).
  • Centering: \(\bar X\) is the full-sample mean, so \(\tau\) is the average effect.
  • estimatr::lm_lin: centers, interacts, and uses HC2 by default.

Freedman (2008), On Regression Adjustments to Experimental Data, Advances in Applied Mathematics 40(2). Lin (2013), Agnostic Notes on Regression Adjustments to Experimental Data, Annals of Applied Statistics 7(1). MacKinnon & White (1985), Some Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimators with Improved Finite Sample Properties, J. Econometrics 29(3).

Simulation: Lin adjustment narrows intervals

  • Covariate: a pretreatment difficulty score for each of the 100 questions.
    • It explains 0% or 80% of the variation across questions.
  • Coverage stays near 95%. Width shrinks when the covariate predicts.

Covariates are fixed before outcomes are seen

  • Pretreatment: measured before assignment, so treatment cannot change it.
    • A pilot difficulty score, question topic, a student’s baseline quiz score.
  • Post-treatment: answer length, number of retrieval calls, time spent with the tutor.
    • Adjusting for these biases the effect estimate.
  • Choose covariates the way you chose blocks: by what predicts the outcome.
  • Name them in the PAP, with the estimator.
    • Trying several sets and reporting the best gives intervals that are too narrow.
  • Blocked designs can adjust too: block indicators as covariates.
  • Gerber & Green (2012), ch. 4: covariates and regression adjustment.
  • Lin (2013), sec. 2.2: poststratification is a special case of interacted adjustment.

Gerber & Green (2012), Field Experiments, ch. 4. Lin (2013), Agnostic Notes on Regression Adjustments to Experimental Data, Annals of Applied Statistics 7(1).

AI predictions as covariates

  • Before the experiment, a model can predict each question’s score.
    • Ask an LLM how hard the question is, or score a cheap model’s answer.
  • Arbour et al.: add the prediction as a covariate in the Lin regression.
lm_lin(Y ~ Z, covariates = ~ pretest + ai_prediction, data = study)
  • Randomization keeps the estimate unbiased however poor the prediction is.
    • A useless prediction gets a coefficient near zero: the difference in means returns.
    • A good prediction narrows the interval.
  • The prediction must use only pretreatment inputs, such as the question text.
  • Schochet: 8 social experiments, median variance reduction ~25%.
  • Shao et al.: 50 biomedical RCTs, median 13% (continuous), 5% (binary).
  • Binary outcomes: adjust for predicted probabilities (log-probs or averaged draws).

Arbour, Ben-Michael, Feller, Lal & Yuan (2026), AI-Assisted Variance Reduction in Randomized Experiments.

Covariate adjustment summary

  • Covariate adjustment buys precision. Randomization already provides unbiasedness.
  • The Lin estimator, with treatment interactions and robust SEs, is at least as precise as the difference in means in large samples.
  • The gain depends on how well the covariate predicts the outcome. A useless covariate costs almost nothing.
  • Only pretreatment covariates qualify, named in the PAP before outcomes are seen. AI predictions built from pretreatment inputs count.

Measured outcomes add uncertainty

What if the scores themselves are off?

  • So far we have trusted the score each answer received.
  • AI judges often do some of the scoring; they make mistakes.
  • Some mistakes only add noise. Others push the result in one direction.
  • This section shows how a small set of human ratings lets you check the judge and correct for it.

LLM-judged outcomes are measured with error

  • Human score \(H_i\): the PAP’s outcome. Judge score \(J_i\): the LLM judge’s score.

\[J_i=H_i+\delta Z_i+u_i.\]

  • \(u_i\): noise independent of treatment. It widens the interval.
  • \(\delta\): error that depends on treatment. Retrieval answers cite sources; the judge rewards citations.
  • The difference in means on \(J\) estimates \(\tau+\delta\).
    • Its SE is correct for the effect on the judge’s score.
    • More questions shrink the interval around \(\tau+\delta\), so coverage of \(\tau\) falls as \(N\) grows.
  • Knox et al.: only a held-out sample of true labels identifies the proxy’s error.
  • Egami et al.: use those true labels to calibrate how the judge’s labels enter the estimate.

Egami, Hinck, Stewart & Wei (2023), Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference, NeurIPS. Knox, Lucas & Cho (2022), Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies, Annual Review of Political Science.

Correct the judge with some human labels

  • The judge scores all \(N\) answers. Humans score a random sample: \(R_i=1\) with known probability \(\pi\), set independently of \(Z_i\).
  • Design-based supervised learning (DSL) pseudo-outcome (Egami et al.):

\[\tilde Y_i=J_i+\frac{R_i}{\pi}\big(H_i-J_i\big),\qquad \hat\tau=\bar{\tilde Y}_1-\bar{\tilde Y}_0.\]

  • \(E[\tilde Y_i\mid H_i,J_i]=H_i\): the correction removes \(\delta\) and all other judge error.
  • Neyman SE on \(\tilde Y\). In one arm with \(N\) answers, \(n=\pi N\) of them human-labeled:

\[V\big(\bar{\tilde Y}\big)=\frac{V(H_i)}{N}+\Big(\frac1n-\frac1N\Big)E\big[(H_i-J_i)^2\big].\]

  • Human labels alone: \(V(H_i)\) replaces \(E[(H_i-J_i)^2]\).
    • The judge helps when its mean squared error is below \(V(H_i)\).

Egami, Hinck, Stewart & Wei (2023), Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference, NeurIPS, eq. 4.

Prediction-powered inference tunes a weight

  • PPI (Boyeau et al.): \(N\) judge scores, \(n\) human labels, and a weight \(\lambda\) on the judge:

\[\hat\mu=\frac{\lambda}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i+\frac1n\sum_{i:R_i=1}\big(H_i-\lambda J_i\big).\]

  • \(\lambda=1\) is the DSL estimate with \(\pi=n/N\).
  • \(\lambda=0\) uses the human labels alone.
  • PPI++ picks \(\lambda\) to minimize the variance, so the estimate is at least as precise as human labels alone.
  • A poor judge makes \(E[(H_i-J_i)^2]\) larger than \(V(H_i)\). Then \(\lambda=1\) is less precise than ignoring the judge.
  • For a treatment effect, apply the estimate in each arm and take the difference.

Boyeau, Angelopoulos, Yosef, Malik & Jordan (2024), AutoEval Done Right, eq. 4.

Simulation: judge-only versus corrected intervals

  • 1,000 questions; the judge scores all and adds \(\delta=2\) to retrieval answers. Humans score a random 5–50%.
  • Judge-only intervals mostly miss. The more accurate judge covers less: a narrower interval around \(\tau+\delta\).
  • Corrected intervals cover. With the 0.95 judge, 10% human labels match the width of 50% labeled by hand.

Correcting judge-scored outcomes

  • An LLM judge is a surrogate for the human score. Judge-only intervals are valid for the effect on the judge’s score.
  • Differential error, where the judge favors one arm, biases the estimate. More questions make the interval more confidently wrong.
  • A random sample of human labels with known probability identifies the judge’s error. DSL and PPI use it to correct the estimate.
  • The corrected interval includes the labeling uncertainty. A more accurate judge needs fewer human labels for the same precision.

Workshop preparation

Plan for missing outcomes and many tests

Missing outcomes

  • Refusals, API errors, timeouts, users who stop.
  • Give every assigned unit an outcome: a refusal or failed call scores as a failure.
    • Then analyze everyone as assigned.
  • Dropping them compares different subsets if treatment changes who goes missing.
  • Fix the retry rule in advance. Report missingness by arm.

Many tests

  • \(k\) independent tests at 5%: the chance of at least one false positive is \(1-0.95^k\), or 40% for \(k=10\).
  • Name one primary outcome. Label the rest secondary or exploratory.
  • For a family of primary tests, adjust the p-values:
    • Holm: familywise error rate.
    • Benjamini–Hochberg: false discovery rate.

Missing data: session 8. Many outcomes and summary indices: session 10. Lin & Green (2016), Standard Operating Procedures: A Safety Net for Pre-Analysis Plans, PS 49(3).

Bring your analysis plan to the workshop

  • Estimand: the effect on which population of questions, users, or annotators, measured on which outcome.
  • Estimator: difference in means, blocked or paired, or Lin with named pretreatment covariates.
  • Standard error: clustered where sampling or assignment groups units; two-way if annotators are sampled.
  • Interval: with few questions or clusters, a \(t\) interval on the CR2 SE or randomization inference. For binary accuracy near 0 or 1, Wilson.
  • Judge-scored outcomes: the fraction humans label at random, and the correction (DSL or PPI++).
  • The workshop also covers missing data (refusals, users who disengage), and multiple comparisons.

Your reflection should trace out a step-by-step analytical recipe that you will follow over all relevant components.
